patent: Filed June 8, 1891 and issued December 22, 1891 to Seth Wheeler of Albany, New York. It covers a roll of toilet paper divided into sheets by cuts across the web that stop short of the center line, so that each sheet hangs from the next by a small tongue that tears easily without ripping into the sheets on either side. The single claim calls this a Λ-shaped tongue; the text also credits the arched, serrated form of the cuts with making the free end easier to find and grip, but does not limit the claim to it. Fig. 1 draws the free end coming over the top of the roll and hanging down in front, and the drawing is widely cited in discussions of which way a roll should hang.

figs.1: Perspective of the roll a with sheets b hanging over the top and down the front. Each zigzag line across the web is one row of cuts: c and c' are lettered on the cuts at the left, c'' and c''' on those at the right, and d at the uncut connection where the cuts rise to a point at the middle. Three such rows are visible: at the top of the roll, partway down the hanging web, and at its torn lower end. e and f are lettered at the center of the roll end and its central hole but are not mentioned in the text.
figs.2: One sheet b after tearing off. The upper edge peaks at d, where the tongue was; the lower edge is notched up at the middle where the tongue of the next sheet tore away. Both left corners are lettered c'; the right corners c''' (upper) and c'' (lower).

parts.d: The claim's Λ-shaped tongue: the narrow strip of paper left between the ends of the cuts, the only bond between sheets.

glossary.def: The continuous strip of paper as it comes off the roll, before it is torn into sheets.
A cut through the paper; here a row of cuts runs in from each side edge but stops short of the center.
Toothed like a saw; the cuts are zigzag, leaving a notched edge on each sheet.
A closing phrase common in claims of this period, tying the claim to the construction set out in the description.
